questions.q: Roughly what percentage of compute cost does a dev/test VM save by running only 8 AM–6 PM on weekdays (50 hours) instead of 24/7 (168 hours)?
options: 0% — hourly billing doesn't change based on uptime
Roughly 70%
100% — the VM stops costing anything at all
Roughly 10%
questions.explain: 50 hours out of 168 is about 30% of the time, so cutting runtime to that window saves roughly 70% of the VM's compute cost.

questions.q: Why does the stop script use Stop-AzVM rather than just shutting down the VM's operating system?
options: Shutting down the OS deletes the VM's disks
Stop-AzVM is required because Azure doesn't allow OS-level shutdown
Stop-AzVM deallocates the VM, releasing the compute hardware so the per-hour billing actually stops
There is no difference between the two approaches
questions.explain: A VM that's only shut down inside the guest OS, without being deallocated, keeps billing for compute — deallocation is what actually stops the charge.

questions.q: What is the purpose of the AutoShutdown tag in this lesson's scripts?
options: It marks which VMs should follow the stop/start schedule, so production VMs without the tag are left alone
It sets the exact time a VM should restart
It is a required Azure system tag with no custom meaning
It replaces the need for a resource group
questions.explain: Get-AzResource filters on the AutoShutdown tag so the schedule only acts on VMs explicitly marked for it, never on untagged production VMs.

questions.q: Why does the stop script include the -Force parameter on Stop-AzVM?
options: -Force has no effect on Stop-AzVM
So the VM is deleted instead of stopped
So the script runs faster by skipping tag lookups
So it doesn't wait on a confirmation prompt that nobody is there to answer when it runs unattended
questions.explain: A switch like -Force skips the interactive confirmation prompt, which matters because this script runs on an unattended schedule, not at a keyboard.

questions.q: How do the stop and start scripts actually run every weekday without anyone triggering them manually?
options: A person must run them manually from PowerShell every day
Azure runs any script placed in the resource group automatically
They're published as Azure Automation runbooks, each attached to its own schedule asset
They run automatically whenever a VM's CPU usage drops
questions.explain: Each script becomes a runbook in Azure Automation, and a schedule asset tells Azure Automation exactly when to fire it — 6 PM for the stop runbook, 8 AM for the start runbook.
